transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Time: 15:00 PT
Duration: 45m
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Singh (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (CTO, Emerald Analytics), Marcus Reed (ML Eng), Sofia Park (Product)

Summary (auto): Hosted API walkthrough — streaming, params, retries, console overview, POC ask

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh this is Alex from Redwood Inference. Priya and I will run through a quick hosted API demo focused on chat and text generation basics. How's that sound?
[00:08] Lena Ortiz: Sounds good, thanks. Quick note, we're on a tight timeline for a POC, so we wanna make sure latency and security checks line up.
[00:14] Alex Chen: Totally, we'll try to hit those; Priya will show some live calls and I'll cover pricing/ops.
[00:22] Priya Singh: Hi all, Priya here. I'll start with a simple text gen example, show streaming, then chat payloads and the SDK.
[00:30] Marcus Reed: Great, Marcus here, I'm mostly interested in batching behavior and how you handle short latency tails.
[00:36] Priya Singh: Perfect. Ok, quick slide — architecture, hosted API is a multi-tenant runtime with optional reserved routes. For demo we'll use the hosted endpoint, model is a 13B open variant in our catalog. 
[00:52] [00:50] Priya Singh: I'm gonna paste a curl call — this is the typical text completion endpoint: POST /v1/generate, you can set max_tokens, temperature, top_p.
[00:58] [01:02] Priya Singh: For streaming we return a server-sent events stream with partial tokens as they generate, so you can render partial UI right away.
[01:12] Sofia Park: So streaming is SSE? Do you support websockets too?
[01:15] Priya Singh: Yep, SSE is the primary streaming mode for the REST API; we do have websocket SDKs in beta for some clients.
[01:22] Marcus Reed: How does retrying work with streaming? If the connection drops mid-stream what happens to idempotency?
[01:28] Alex Chen: Good question. Redwood supports idempotency keys on requests; for streaming we also return a final tokenized offset so a resumed request can skip already-delivered tokens. If you can't resume, we recommend retrying against a smaller window or re-requesting with the same idempotency key — the server uses the key to dedupe generation.
[01:45] Lena Ortiz: Is that documented? We'll need that for our SRE team.
[01:48] Alex Chen: Yeah, Priya will drop the link to the docs and the sample SDK code.
[01:51] [02:00] Priya Singh: Ok demo time — I'm running a quick JS SDK example. Code: const resp = await client.generate({model: "redwood-13b-open", prompt: "Summarize product feedback", temperature: 0.7, max_tokens: 150, stream: true});
[02:16] [02:18] Priya Singh: You can see the stream events come in, each chunk includes token delta and approximate token count for billing.
[02:26] Marcus Reed: Where do you calculate token counts? On the edge or in the control plane?
[02:30] Priya Singh: Tokenization occurs at the edge before the request hits the runtime, so the token estimate you see in the stream is close to final billing. There's small variance for special tokens.
[02:42] [03:00] Lena Ortiz: Our primary requirement is predictable cost per request; can you show the Console cost breakdown?
[03:07] Priya Singh: Sure, switching to Console — here we have per-route dashboards, token-level cost, latency percentile charts, and model usage. You can set per-route rate limits and quotas.
[03:22] Alex Chen: Customers often use model pinning for predictable spend — pin to a quantized variant or lower-cost model for certain routes.
[03:30] Sofia Park: What's the unit pricing cadence? Per 1k tokens? Do you charge separately for embeddings?
[03:35] Alex Chen: Yes, hosted pricing is per 1k tokens for generation and per-embedding unit for embeddings; we'll include exact numbers in the pricing doc.
[03:43] [04:00] Marcus Reed: On batching — if we send many short requests, will Redwood batch them server-side to improve throughput?
[04:07] Priya Singh: We do continuous batching in the runtime. For short requests you'll see improved GPU utilization and lower per-token cost. You can configure expected latency SLOs; the router will decide how aggressive batching can be.
[04:20] Marcus Reed: Any control over batching window?
[04:23] Priya Singh: Exposed as a hint in Dedicated and via policy in Reserved routes; in hosted we provide suggested config and AutoBatching handles it. We'll share recommended params.
[04:35] [05:00] Lena Ortiz: Security questions: SOC 2, encryption at rest, KMS integration for private deployments?
[05:07] Alex Chen: Redwood is SOC 2 Type II. Hosted customers can request a data retention window; for sensitive workloads we recommend Private (VPC) deployment which integrates with your KMS/HSM. We have SAML SSO and RBAC for the Console.
[05:22] Lena Ortiz: Can you prevent data from being used for model training?
[05:26] Alex Chen: Yes, hosted enterprise accounts can opt out of data usage for training — we have contractual provisions and technical controls. Priya will attach the security whitepaper.
[05:38] [06:00] Sofia Park: For the POC, we plan to test latency at 99th pctl and cost per 1k tokens on our dataset. What do you need from us?
[06:09] Priya Singh: Ideally a representative sample payload set, expected concurrency, and any max sequence lengths. We'll run benchmarks and share results.
[06:18] Marcus Reed: Also curious about fallback policies — if a model is overloaded can requests be routed to a cheaper variant automatically?
[06:24] Alex Chen: Yes, smart routing supports fallback to pinned variants or lower-capacity Tiers, with automatic schema compatibility checks. You can define policy: latency-first or cost-first.
[06:36] [07:00] Priya Singh: Back to demo — here's a chat example payload: messages array with roles user/system/assistant, plus function calling options. Setting stream:true returns partial assistant tokens.
[07:16] Priya Singh: Note on params: temperature controls randomness, top_p does nucleus sampling, max_tokens is cap, stop sequences supported. For chat contexts we also expose token_window and advise keeping a rolling context plus KV cache for embeddings for retrieval augmentation.
[07:34] Marcus Reed: How big is the KV cache? If we keep long running chats what's the impact?
[07:40] Priya Singh: The runtime keeps a KV cache per session up to configured size; for hosted we recommend summarization or retrieval augmentation after ~8k tokens to avoid high costs. Dedicated customers can tune cache size.
[07:53] [08:00] Lena Ortiz: Retries — what's your recommended approach for client-side retry logic when calls fail with 5xx or network errors?
[08:08] Alex Chen: We recommend an idempotency key for non-streamed requests, exponential backoff with jitter for HTTP 5xx, and avoid automatic retries for streaming unless you handle resume via the stream offset. Our SDKs implement smart default retry policies you can override.
[08:26] Marcus Reed: Do you surface error reasons in the response body? e.g., model overloaded, rate limited, token limit exceeded?
[08:33] Priya Singh: Yes error payloads include an error.code and error.detail. For rate limits we return Retry-After headers and a structured JSON error.
[08:45] [09:00] Sofia Park: Any built-in request validation? We want to prevent accidental huge token bills.
[09:05] Alex Chen: You can enable per-route max_tokens caps and soft warnings in the Console. Also set per-key quotas.
[09:15] [10:00] Priya Singh: Quick note on streaming: each SSE event includes a delta, a cumulative token_count, and an event_id. If the client reconnects with the last event_id, the server can resume from the next token. There are edge cases with sampling nondeterminism so we advise testing resume behavior for your UI.
[10:36] Marcus Reed: Good to know. For our POC we'd like a script to simulate 200 rps of short chats — can you help run that?
[10:43] Priya Singh: Yes, we'll share a benchmark harness. We can run it from our infra or you can run against trial keys — depends on your preference.
[10:51] [12:00] Alex Chen: Ok I'm going to share a couple of links in the meeting chat: pricing sheet, security whitepaper, SDK examples, and the benchmark harness repo.
[12:12] [12:35] Lena Ortiz: On data residency, we operate in EU and NA — can you commit to EU-only processing?
[12:40] Alex Chen: We have region pinning for requests; hosted EU regions process data in EU. For strict residency we recommend Private deployment. We'll include region options in the proposal.
[12:52] [14:00] Priya Singh: Also small gotcha — streaming can increase perceived latency because you render partial tokens, but it reduces time-to-first-byte. For some UI patterns batching a few tokens on client-side helps.
[14:20] Marcus Reed: What about model quantization — any impact on output quality?
[14:26] Priya Singh: We provide quantized variants with small quality delta; we'll share evaluation benchmarks comparing 8-bit/4-bit quantized models vs fp16. Use-cases with heavy factuality needs we recommend a higher-precision variant.
[14:45] [16:00] Sofia Park: Can you show an example of a retryable error and how to handle it in the SDK?
[16:06] Priya Singh: Sure — example in Python: use client.generate(..., idempotency_key="uuid"), wrap call in try/except, on network error call client.resume_stream(idempotency_key, last_event_id) or fallback to a re-run with same key for non-stream. SDKs return structured exceptions.
[16:28] [18:00] Alex Chen: Customers also use our Console to set automated fallbacks: if a route crosses a latency threshold it can route to a lower-cost model or move to a degraded mode that returns cached or stubbed responses.
[18:12] Lena Ortiz: That could work for us. Our key success criteria for the POC: 99p latency < 800ms for short chat (<=64 tokens), cost under $X per 1k tokens — we'll define X in follow-up.
[18:24] Alex Chen: Great — we'll include those as acceptance criteria.
[18:30] [20:00] Priya Singh: Wrapping up demo — link to SDK snippets, streaming resume docs, and batching recommendations in chat.
[20:10] [20:30] Lena Ortiz: Thanks. A couple quick questions from security: what's your retention default and how do we request deletion?
[20:38] Alex Chen: Hosted default is 30 days for enterprise trial, but enterprise or private customers can set retention to 0 days and require immediate deletion or instrument retention via the Console. We'll include deletion SLA info in the security whitepaper.
[20:52] Marcus Reed: Last one — do you support structured output like function calling?
[20:56] Priya Singh: Yes function calling supported; you can declare schemas and the model will return structured JSON. Works with streaming too, but you get partial JSON chunks. We recommend assembling on client and validating schema at end.
[21:14] [22:00] Alex Chen: Ok let's recap real quick. Action items: Alex sends pricing and trial instructions; Priya shares benchmark harness and SDK examples; customer shares sample payloads and SSO contact. Agreed to schedule POC kickoff next week.
[22:18] Lena Ortiz: Sounds good. We'll aim to have the dataset and admin contact by 2026-03-08.
[22:25] Sofia Park: Thanks everyone, this was helpful.
[22:30] Alex Chen: Thanks all — we'll follow up with docs and a calendar invite.
[22:35] [End of recording]
